title: Psalm 76: God Known in Judah, Feared by Kings
summary: The psalm celebrates God, who dwells in Zion and has shattered the weapons of war there. Mighty warriors lie in their last sleep and horse and rider are stunned at his rebuke. God rises to judge and to save the lowly of the earth, and the nations are called to bring tribute to him who is feared by the kings of the earth.
story: Psalm 75 announced that God would judge at the time he chooses; Psalm 76 celebrates a moment when he has already done so, breaking an enemy's power at Jerusalem. It belongs with the songs of Zion, psalms like 46 and 48 that celebrate God's presence in his city and his defense of it against hostile armies. After the ruined sanctuary of Psalm 74, this psalm remembers a time when the city stood and the attackers fell, which gives the people ground for hope. It also looks outward, calling the surrounding nations to acknowledge Israel's God.
historical: The heading reads “For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments. A Psalm of Asaph. A song.” For Asaph and his guild, see Psalm 73. The psalm describes a dramatic defeat of an army at Jerusalem, and many interpreters connect it with the Assyrian king Sennacherib's campaign against Judah in 701 BC. According to 2 Kings 19:35-36 and Isaiah 37:36-37, the angel of the LORD struck down the Assyrian camp, and Sennacherib withdrew to Nineveh. The Greek translation of the psalm adds a note to the heading connecting it with the Assyrian, showing that this reading is ancient. Other scholars see the psalm as a liturgical celebration of God's kingship over Zion that doesn't refer to one battle but to a pattern of divine protection, perhaps used at a festival. The psalm itself names no event, so both views remain open.
cultural:
Salem (verse 2) is an older, poetic name for Jerusalem; it appears in Genesis 14:18 as the city of Melchizedek, and the name is related to the Hebrew word for peace. The word for God's tent or dwelling in verse 2 can also mean a lair, and the image may be of God as a lion in his den, going out to defend his territory (verse 4 speaks of mountains filled with game, which some read as mountains of prey).

The weapons of verse 3 describe the arsenal of ancient warfare: flaming arrows (literally flashes of the bow), shields, swords, and weapons of battle. Chariot horses were the most feared military force of the day, and the stunned horse and rider in verse 6 echo the song Israel sang after the exodus, when horse and rider were thrown into the sea (Exodus 15:1). Vows (verse 11) were promises to offer a sacrifice or gift to God, usually made in time of trouble and fulfilled after deliverance. Tribute was paid by subject nations to a great king as a sign of submission.
literary: The psalm has four short stanzas, with Selah after the first and the third, a musical or liturgical marker whose exact meaning is unknown. Verses 1 to 3 locate God in Judah, Israel, Salem, and Zion and describe the weapons he broke there. Verses 4 to 6 address God directly and describe the defeated warriors. Verses 7 to 9 ask who can stand before him and describe his judgment from heaven. Verses 10 to 12 call for vows and tribute. The key word is fear (yare), which appears in verses 7, 8, 11, and 12, and the psalm moves outward from Judah to the earth and its kings. Verse 10 is difficult in Hebrew, and translations differ on how the wrath of man praises God.

outline.t: God is known in Judah and dwells in Zion
The mighty lie stunned at God's rebuke
Who can stand before him? God rises to judge
Vows and tribute to the God who is feared

doctrines.note: God's judgment in this psalm has a clear purpose: to save all the lowly of the earth (verse 9). His power against the mighty is exercised on behalf of the weak.
Kings, princes, and armies are no match for God. He breaks the spirits of princes, and even human wrath is made to serve his praise.
The repeated call to fear God expresses awe at his majesty and power. No one can stand before him when he is angry, and the right response is reverent worship.

words.note: Yare, to fear. It appears in verses 7, 8, and 12 (with the related noun mora in verse 11). In the Old Testament the fear of God is not mere terror but reverent awe that leads to worship and obedience. Here even the earth and its kings fear him.

Shalem, Salem. A poetic name for Jerusalem, first mentioned as the city of Melchizedek, king and priest (Genesis 14:18). Its sound recalls shalom, peace, a fitting name for the city where God breaks the weapons of war.

Anav, poor, humble, or lowly. In verse 9 God rises to judge in order to save the lowly of the earth. The word often describes people who are oppressed and who depend on God, and it becomes a key term for the faithful poor in the Psalms and the prophets.

christ: Psalm 76 isn't quoted in the New Testament, and its connection with Jesus is thematic. Salem recalls Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, whom Hebrews presents as a picture of Christ's kingship and priesthood (Hebrews 7:1-3). God's shattering of weapons in Zion anticipates the hope that the Messiah will bring peace to the nations and end war (Isaiah 2:4; Zechariah 9:9-10), which the New Testament connects with Jesus entering Jerusalem as a humble king. Jesus also taught that the meek will inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5), echoing the psalm's picture of a God who judges to save the lowly. Revelation pictures the kings of the earth bringing their glory into the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:24), the final form of the tribute this psalm calls for.
questions: The psalm says God rose to judge to save the lowly of the earth. How does that shape the way you think about God's judgment?
What powers or threats seem overwhelming to you right now, and what would it mean to see them in light of this psalm?
Verse 11 calls people to make and keep vows to God. What promises have you made to God, and how are you keeping them?
